summary: TerraRoute is a free web app that helps farmers explore crop rotations that protect their soil and fit a changing climate. A farmer picks their location, enters their crop history, soil, water access and priorities, and TerraRoute retrieves 25 years of NASA POWER data for that exact point: rainfall, temperature, sunlight and root-zone soil wetness. It turns these numbers into a simple month-by-month risk calendar that shows when the field sits bare, and when crops face dry spells, frost or extreme heat. It then compares the farmer’s current rotation with two alternatives, such as a winter cover crop or a nitrogen-fixing legume, and lets them stress-test every option under hotter, drier or wetter conditions. Each suggestion explains the NASA evidence behind it, its trade-offs and what still needs checking locally. This matters because rotation decisions are made once a season and are hard to undo, yet most farmers have no easy way to see long-term climate data for their own field. TerraRoute makes that data readable, while leaving the final decision with farmers and local experts.
details:
What does it do?

TerraRoute is a free web app that helps farmers explore crop rotations that protect their soil and suit their local climate. It guides them through six steps:

  1. Your farm: choose a location on the map or type coordinates anywhere in the world, then enter crop history (with planting and harvest dates), soil, water access, equipment, market access and priorities.
  2. Weather and water: see an “average year at your farm” built from 25 years of NASA data, comparing rainfall with the water crops need, alongside soil wetness and plain-language takeaways.
  3. Vulnerable periods: a colour-coded 12-month risk calendar shows bare-soil, dry, frost, heat and soil-wetness months at a glance.
  4. Rotation choices: the current rotation is compared with two alternatives, each with a 12-month crop calendar, a climate-fit rating and data-based indicators (months covered, rain on bare soil, crop diversity, extra water demand).
  5. Hotter, drier or wetter: each option is stress-tested under +2 °C, −20% rain, +20% rain or custom conditions, with a plain-language verdict.
  6. Explain and save: every option shows its evidence, trade-offs, risks and information gaps, and the farmer can download a farm summary or a full technical report.

How does it work?

  • The app requests daily data from the NASA POWER API for the farmer’s exact coordinates (2001–2025): temperature (T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN), rainfall (PRECTOTCORR), sunlight (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN) and soil wetness (GWETTOP, GWETROOT).
    • Iowa corn/soybean farms get locally reviewed examples based on Iowa State University Extension guidance and a published Iowa field study (Davis et al., 2012).
    • Every other location gets a general climate screen that tests cover crops, legumes and drought-tolerant crops against that farm’s NASA temperatures and frost risk. Poor fits are never suggested, and these options are clearly labelled “not locally reviewed”.
    • Options that conflict with the farmer’s constraints, such as no equipment or no market, are removed and the reason is shown.
  • Regional context comes from a NASA POWER state temperature map, and a 2024 MODIS NDVI series (via AppEEARS) shows vegetation for the Ames, Iowa sample farm.

What benefits does it have?

  • Turns decades of NASA Earth observations into something a farmer can understand in seconds, without needing data or GIS skills.
  • Works for any location on Earth. We tested farms in Iowa, Minnesota, California and northeast Thailand.
  • Shows the why behind every suggestion, including the actual NASA numbers, so farmers can judge for themselves.
  • Honest about uncertainty: it never predicts yields, profit or guaranteed water savings, and it flags what needs local checking.
  • Free, runs in any web browser, and works on phones.

What is the intended impact?

We want TerraRoute to start better conversations between farmers, extension officers and agronomists. It doesn’t tell farmers what to plant. It helps them spot long bare-soil periods, dry or hot months, and rotation ideas they may not have considered, backed by evidence they can check. Over time, this could help reduce erosion, build soil health and make farms more resilient to changing weather. Future versions could add satellite soil moisture (SMAP), rainfall intensity (GPM IMERG), field-level vegetation (Landsat and Sentinel-2) and locally reviewed crop lists for more regions.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Language: Python
  • Libraries: Streamlit (web app), pandas and NumPy (data processing), Plotly (charts and maps), Requests (NASA POWER API), openpyxl (spreadsheets)
  • Development: GitHub for teamwork and version control; GitHub Codespaces and VS Code for coding
  • Hosting: Streamlit Community Cloud (free, public)
  • AI assistance: AI coding assistants helped write and refactor code and draft interface text. The idea and design are our team’s own.
  • Hardware: none. TerraRoute runs entirely in the browser.

How is the project creative?

  • Instead of a crowded dashboard, TerraRoute tells the story of one farm: what the land goes through in an average year, where the gaps are, and what could fill them.
  • The risk calendar and the crop-calendar strip on each option make complex climate data visual and easy to compare.
  • The stress test lets farmers ask “what if it gets hotter or drier?” and see how each rotation holds up.
  • Small honest touches: a winter cover crop dormant under snow still counts as protecting the soil, but it’s labelled “dormant” rather than growing.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Farmers first: plain language, colour-coded visuals, a three-step how-to guide, and technical detail kept in expandable sections.
  • Scientific honesty: NASA data is regional (about a 50 km grid) and modelled, not a field sensor. Soil wetness is not a soil test, and scenarios are sensitivity tests, not forecasts. The app says so wherever it matters.
  • Supporting local expertise: every option ends with what to check locally before trying it.
  • Reliability: if the live NASA request fails, the app switches to a saved NASA record for the sample farm and says so clearly.
  • Competition rules: no NASA logos or branding, and AI use is disclosed in the project files.
dataRefs: U.S. Geological Survey (Landsat and MODIS/ VIIRS)
NASA Global Precipitation Measurement Mission (GPM and IMERG)
NASA Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER)
